title: Boss: on call
summary: Three on-call tickets on a real Kubernetes cluster: read a namespace's events, unstick a Pending workload, and close an RBAC hole.

steps.title: The scene
body: You are on call. Each ticket opens its own one-node **Kubernetes 1.37** cluster with the problem already there. The
`kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o wide` and `kubectl auth can-i --as`.

steps.title: Ticket 1: what happened in shop this morning?
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). Five pods in the namespace `shop`, and a bad morning. Use the **events** (sorted by time) to
answer, one pod name per file:
1. `~/answers/pull.txt`: the pod whose image cannot be pulled;
2. `~/answers/schedule.txt`: the pod the scheduler cannot place;
3. `~/answers/probe.txt`: the pod whose readiness probe fails;

checks.name: pull.txt
checks.fail: Not the pod with the pull failure (`Failed`, `ErrImagePull` / `BackOff pulling image`).

checks.name: schedule.txt
checks.cmd: test "$(xargs < ~/answers/schedule.txt)" = "$(kubectl -n shop get events -o json | jq -r '[.items[] | select(.involvedObject.kind=="Pod" and .reason=="FailedScheduling") | .involvedObject.name] | unique | join(" ")')"

checks.name: probe.txt
checks.cmd: test "$(xargs < ~/answers/probe.txt)" = "$(kubectl -n shop get events -o json | jq -r '[.items[] | select(.involvedObject.kind=="Pod" and .reason=="Unhealthy") | .involvedObject.name] | unique | join(" ")')"
checks.fail: Not the pod with `Unhealthy` (Readiness probe failed).

checks.name: crash.txt
checks.fail: Not the pod in a crash loop (`BackOff: Back-off restarting failed container`).

hints: `kubectl -n shop get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp` lists REASON and OBJECT for everything that happened.
Filter one kind: `kubectl -n shop get events --field-selector reason=FailedScheduling`; or `kubectl events -n shop --types=Warning`.
Image pulls: `Failed` with `ErrImagePull`; scheduling: `FailedScheduling`; probes: `Unhealthy`; crashes: `BackOff ... restarting failed container`.
steps.explain: Events are Kubernetes' own log of what it did and what went wrong, per object: the scheduler, the kubelet and the controllers all write them. `--sort-by=.lastTimestamp` turns them into a timeline, and the REASON column (`FailedScheduling`, `Failed`, `Unhealthy`, `BackOff`, `OOMKilling`) is usually the whole diagnosis. They are kept for only about an hour, so ship them somewhere if you want them for post-mortems.

steps.title: Ticket 2: the indexer never starts
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). `indexer` has been `Pending` since it was deployed. The node `dojo` is in the `general` pool for now
(`kubectl get nodes --show-labels`), and the platform team says batch work may run there until the batch pool exists.
Make `indexer` run on `dojo` **without relabelling the node**.

checks.name: indexer runs
checks.cmd: kubectl rollout status deploy/indexer --timeout=40s >/dev/null; kubectl get deploy indexer -o jsonpath='{.status.readyReplicas}'

checks.name: the node keeps its labels
checks.fail: Do not relabel the node: change where `indexer` asks to run.

hints: `kubectl describe pod -l app=indexer` (or the events): `didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector`.
The pod asks for `pool: batch`; the node is `pool: general`.
steps.explain: `Pending` has only a few causes, and the `FailedScheduling` event names them: not enough resources, a `nodeSelector`/affinity that no node matches, taints the pod does not tolerate, or a volume that cannot be attached in that zone. Selectors are the quiet one: the YAML is valid, the pod simply waits forever for a node that does not exist.

steps.title: Ticket 3: close the RBAC hole
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). Security's audit says a **workload's** service account can do anything in the cluster.
1. Find the ClusterRoleBinding that grants `cluster-admin` to a service account, write its name into
2. Leave the legitimate bindings alone: `web` keeps read-only access to its own namespace, the deployer keeps `edit`
in `shop`, and Prometheus keeps reading metrics.

checks.name: binding.txt names the dangerous binding
checks.fail: Not the binding. `kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o wide` shows each one's role and subjects.

checks.name: shop's web account is no longer an admin
checks.cmd: kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' --all-namespaces --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:web; kubectl auth can-i list pods -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:web
checks.fail: `shop:web` should not be cluster-admin any more, but should still `list pods` in `shop` (its `view` RoleBinding).

checks.name: the other grants still work
checks.cmd: kubectl auth can-i patch deployments -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:deployer; kubectl auth can-i list nodes --as=system:serviceaccount:monitoring:prometheus
checks.fail: Do not remove the deployer's or Prometheus's bindings.

hints: `kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o wide | grep cluster-admin` lists who has it (ignore the built-in `system:` subjects).
`kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.roleRef.name=="cluster-admin") | .metadata.name + " " + ([.subjects[]? | .kind + ":" + .name] | join(","))'`.
`kubectl delete clusterrolebinding web-debug-tmp`, then check with `kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:web`.
solution: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.roleRef.name=="cluster-admin") | .metadata.name + " " + ([.subjects[]? | .kind + ":" + .name] | join(","))'
steps.explain: Every pod runs as a service account, and its token is mounted into the pod by default, so a workload bound to `cluster-admin` means "anyone who exploits this web app owns the cluster". Temporary debug grants are the classic source. Audits look for cluster-admin, wildcard verbs, `secrets` access and `bind`/`escalate`; for apps that do not call the API at all, `automountServiceAccountToken: false` removes the token entirely.
